De’Aaron Fox isn’t dwelling on past, only getting back to NBA Finals

Healthy and motivated, San Antonio Spurs guard explains why he played hurt against New York Knicks

Marc J. Spears @MarcJSpears
October 14, 2026
Topics:
De'Aaron Fox NBA San Antonio Spurs Sports

SALT LAKE CITY — As loud as it was in Madison Square Garden when De’Aaron Fox’s layup was blocked in the final seconds of Game 4 of the 2026 NBA Finals, the criticism on sports talk platforms and social media toward the San Antonio Spurs guard was even louder.

His misses and miscues were recalled repeatedly. There was also wild trade speculation. Widely overlooked, however, was the painful high ankle sprain that Fox played through in pursuit of his first NBA championship.

Somehow, Fox was unfazed and mostly unaware of all the social-media noise and sports-talk smoke.

“I don’t have basketball on my timeline,” Fox said. “No one is calling me talking. I can’t do nothing about all the other things. Everybody has a podcast. Everyone thinks their opinion matters. …

“This is my first time in the conference finals and the Finals. There is no way I can’t play right now. If it were the regular season, I definitely wouldn’t have played.”

Fox averaged 18.6 points, 6.2 assists and 3.8 rebounds per game last season for San Antonio. He also flourished in the first round against the Portland Trail Blazers and the first four games of a second-round series against the Minnesota Timberwolves.

However, the 2026 NBA All-Star suffered a right high ankle sprain during Game 4 against the Timberwolves. The injury typically keeps an NBA player out between four and six weeks.

“I was the second-leading scorer when I got hurt,” Fox said.

Fox, however, didn’t have the typical mentality toward his injury — given his playoff history, and with the Spurs aiming for their first NBA Finals appearance since 2014, he kept playing.

The 28-year-old’s only prior postseason appearance was a first-round exit as a member of the Sacramento Kings in 2023. There were no guarantees he would ever get another opportunity to play for a championship. Fox drew inspiration from Indiana Pacers guard Tyrese Haliburton, who played through a calf strain in the 2025 NBA Finals, only to suffer a torn Achilles tendon in a deciding Game 7 loss.

“Why did I play? I felt like I could help the team,” Fox said. “Seeing the OKC [conference finals] series, I thought there were things I could come out there and help with. If you ask any player — and you could use Tyrese as the biggest [example] for that — you know there is a chance you could get hurt if you have a calf strain. And he was like, ‘Oh, this is Game 7 of the Finals. And for me, there is nothing more I want to do than play in this game.’

“This is my first time being in the conference finals, first time being in the Finals. So, of course I want to play.”

Fox played in the final two games of the Spurs’ second-round series against the Timberwolves but missed the first two games of the Western Conference finals against the Oklahoma City Thunder. He played in the remaining five games of the conference finals, helping the Spurs to a seven-game win.

It was obvious Fox was hampered against the Thunder, averaging just 11.2 points per game on 36.5% shooting from the field and 22.7% from 3-point range in the series.

“I played more games in the playoffs hurt than I did healthy,” Fox said from the Spurs’ shootaround Monday morning from Delta Center in preparation for a preseason game. “It is what it is. It happened. People can talk. It’s no sweat off my back.”

Fox, All-Star center Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs opened as high as -220 favorites to win the 2026 NBA Finals. Before Game 1, Fox said his right high ankle sprain did not feel great, but he was able to play. With a first-ever title at stake, he had no intention of missing out due to injury. The Spurs did not take him out of the starting lineup either.

Looking back, Spurs head coach Mitch Johnson said it was a collective franchise decision to keep Fox on the floor.

“There is a lot of conversation that happens within our walls that we keep within our walls,” Johnson said. “And obviously, when you start talking about people’s health and availability, typically there is the player and everyone around who is trying to support him.

“And you trust that people’s opinions and voices in those moments all want the same thing — that is, the best thing for the player to try to help the team. And that doesn’t always mean it’s the same answer.”

In Game 1 of the Finals, Fox still wasn’t the All-Star version of himself. He scored seven points while missing 10 of 13 shots and all four of his 3-point attempts during a 105-95 loss to the New York Knicks in Game 1 in San Antonio.

It was evident his athleticism and quickness were hampered. He scored 20 points in a Game 2 loss in San Antonio but managed just 12 points while going 0-for-5 from 3-point range in a Game 3 win in New York.

The Spurs entered Game 4 down 2-1 in the best-of-seven series. San Antonio, however, seemed primed to even the series, taking a 76-49 lead into halftime at Madison Square Garden in New York after hitting 14 3-pointers. But the Knicks mounted a historic 29-point comeback to win 107-106 and take a commanding series lead.

Fox received much of the blame for the collapse. He missed six of eight shots and committed two turnovers on a team-high 44 second-half touches, while also making a critical mistake near the end of the game.

With the Spurs up one point with about 13 seconds left and the shot clock off, Fox had the ball on a fast break with options.

He could have attempted to dribble out the clock or wait for the Knicks to foul him and send him to the free throw line, or attempt a layup that could put his team up three. Fox decided to try to outrun Knicks forward OG Anunoby for a layup that he may have dunked under normal, healthy conditions.

Instead, Anunoby ran Fox down and blocked the shot, giving the Knicks possession with about 11 seconds left. While a replay later showed a potential foul by Anunoby, it wasn’t called.

“I’ve definitely thought about it,” Fox said about the sequence. “It happened. Obviously, knowing the outcome I’d definitely try to play it differently. It happened. I can’t say I thought about it in the past month as we’ve gotten ready for this season. But I thought about it over the summer, for sure.”

And after Knicks star Jalen Brunson missed a 3-pointer on the ensuing possession, Anunoby stunned the NBA world with a game-winning tip-in with 1.3 seconds left. The incredible comeback victory gave New York control of the series with a 3-1 lead, and the Knicks went on to beat the Spurs in Game 5 in San Antonio to win their first NBA title since 1973.

Of all the Spurs players, no one drew more criticism than Fox after it ended.

However, Fox earned even more respect from Johnson for fighting through ankle pain in an attempt to help the Spurs win.

“De’Aaron Fox has proven throughout his career, before he got to us and with us, that he is a tough, durable player,” Johnson said. “When you look back at the playoffs in totality, when you look at the Minnesota series, the Oklahoma City series and into the Finals, he proved exactly that. Nothing has changed there.

“There are a lot of things that get more attention when you get further into the playoffs. Rightfully so. That’s the business that we’re in. That is how this thing works. It probably comes with more praise than it deserves and more criticism than is probably true.”

Fox and his family spent most of the offseason in his native Houston and also vacationed in Jamaica. As time passed, he mostly moved on mentally from his Finals struggles, and his ankle healed.

“My mentality on vacation was to get healthy and work — the same as any summer,” Fox said. “I reflected [on the Finals] a bit. But at some point, you have to move on. It took two months. It took a while. But you don’t want to just sit here and dwell on that, knowing you have another season to get ready for. …

“It is what it is. It happened. I’m not going to sit around here thinking about things that happened years ago. So, I’m not going to sit and think about things that happened months ago.”

The Spurs and the Thunder have +270 to +500 odds to win the 2027 NBA Finals, according to ESPN NBA Futures. The Spurs are also expected to employ a new three-guard starting lineup featuring Fox, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper.

While Fox knows there is a long, unexpected road to go, he believes the Spurs’ painful Finals experience from last season will be quite valuable this time around. He also believes the road back to the Finals will be tougher as Western Conference champions, because they will get “everyone’s best shot.”

“We want to get back to where we were, but it’s a long season,” Fox said. “I don’t know how many teams that have been to the Finals the last six or seven years has been back to the Finals. That’s our goal. But we know we have to take it one game at a time. …

“We’ve gotten better. Being able to get to that position [last season], we understand what it takes. But we can’t get bored with the regular season, because we can put ourselves in a tough position to get back there. A lot of teams don’t get back there.”

Marc J. Spears is the senior NBA writer for Andscape. He used to be able to dunk on you, but he hasn’t been able to in years and his knees still hurt.

Brian Flores, NFL coach hiring and systemic racism hiding in plain sight

Recruiting firm report shows stereotypes, double standards Black coaches face

William C. Rhoden @RhodenRhoden8
October 15, 2026
Topics:
Brian Flores Commentary Locker Room Talk Minnesota Vikings NFL Sports

    By Cliff Brunt

    By Jason Reid
  • Share on X (Opens in new window) X
  • Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook
  • Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email

For the past three seasons, football fans have become accustomed to hearing praise lavished on Brian Flores for his work as defensive coordinator of the Minnesota Vikings.

The “Brian Flores Defense” has become a trademark that means creative, nonstop blitzes, perpetual attack mode. On the sidelines, Flores is an animated figure — edgy, intense, exhorting the defense to wreak mayhem.

The Vikings are undefeated, their defense is dominant, and fans almost forgot that Flores is suing the NFL. They got a reminder earlier this week, when the public learned that a recruiting report, prepared by the firm Korn Ferry for the Las Vegas Raiders during a recent coaching search, was unsealed as part of Flores’ discrimination suit against multiple NFL teams.

The report, first made public by Front Office Sports, included an assessment of Flores that revealed stereotypical thinking is alive and well.

After lauding Flores for his defensive acumen, the report said Flores was “polished and a good presenter.” The problem is that the platitudes were followed by a disparaging disclaimer: “despite growing up in Brownsville, Brooklyn.”

The report commended Flores for cultivating a relationship with the son of a billionaire, which in turn allowed him opportunities to socialize and learn how to build relationships with white-collar and upper-class individuals. In other words, thanks to his proximity to whiteness, Flores was able to overcome his Black inner-city roots.

The report also said Flores “can fool you with his polish,” had little people skills, lacks self-awareness, and can sometimes exhibit “erratic behavior.” The assessment noted Flores could be a “dictator with players, coaches,” and could be “difficult with ownership.” It called Flores’ personality “unpredictable,” concluding he “needs someone strong at the top to reign [sic] in some of his worst behavior.”

For all of the excitement of the NFL season, the Vikings’ early success and praise heaped on Flores, the recruitment report reminds us why Flores, a former Miami Dolphins head coach, filed his class action suit in the first place. Filed in 2022, the suit attacks systemic racism. In an atmosphere of hostility toward diversity, equity and inclusion, and denials that systemic racism even exists, Flores’ suit argues that such racism does exist, perhaps more now than ever.

Recruitment reports are supposed to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of potential coaching candidates, and Flores has been criticized in the past for how he dealt with players while he was in Miami.

Atlanta Falcons backup quarterback Tua Tagovailoa, who played in Miami under Flores, said the coach had a negative impact on his self-confidence. According to Tagovailoa, Flores repeatedly told him he didn’t belong it the NFL. Flores never apologized to Tagovailoa but did say there were things he could have done better in Miami.

But the issue here is stereotypes and double standards. For a white NFL head coach, being called a dictator and difficult is a badge of honor that speaks to toughness and commitment. For an African American candidate, those descriptions become a negative.

Who creates the standard, and are the standards applied to everyone? Black candidates often carry assumptions that would not be attached to their white counterparts.

Related Story

The resurgence of Brian Flores – Andscape Read now

The recruitment report said Flores was polished.

“Polished” is ordinarily a compliment, but the recruitment report said, “polished despite.” Polish was unexpected from a Black man from Brownsville. Brownsville, where roughly two-thirds of the population is Black and another 20% is Latino, was shorthand for a deficit.

Flores’ friendship with a wealthy white man allowed him to overcome his deficiencies and circulate in a white world. The search firm’s comments about Flores were not just about his acumen as a defensive coordinator, but about his background, where he came from, and how he was able to rise from a flawed upbringing and develop class and polish.

Whoever wrote the report will say in his or her own defense that the wording was not meant as a slur or to be hostile. Some of the other terms — “difficult,” “unpredictable,” or “needs someone strong to rein him in” — would be a positive reflection of a white candidate’s intensity, conviction and high standards.

Who makes these determinations, and how do these subjective suppositions impact hiring decisions?

News of the recruitment report came a few days before a TV station in Charlotte, North Carolina, reported that a text thread among some Charlotte-Mecklenburg police officers included a competition over who could pull over the Blackest drivers.

There is a connection between the search firm stereotyping a Black head coaching candidate and law enforcement targeting Black drivers.

In each case, Blackness was part of the evaluation. With Flores, a Black coach’s personality and intelligence was filtered through the prism of stereotypes. In North Carolina, Black drivers became targets for a contest by law enforcement officials.

Both are examples of precisely what is meant by systemic racism. The Flores example occurred in the context of hiring, the Black drivers in the exercise of authority. One purports to measure merit, the other purports to serve the public trust. Both underline the consequences of institutions making racial assumptions.

The purpose of Flores’ lawsuit is to force the NFL to re-examine its hiring process for head coaches and leadership positions. But the recruiting report is larger than the Flores lawsuit or even whether Flores gets another head coaching job.

This is about language, perception and double-standard stereotypes, all of which have been used to maintain the status quo. Who is allowed to be demanding without being characterized as a dictator or overbearing? Who is allowed to be confident without being called arrogant?

It’s good Flores is going through with his lawsuit and that the details will be public. He just may blitz the NFL into fair play.

William C. Rhoden is a columnist for Andscape and the author of Forty Million Dollar Slaves: The Rise, Fall, and Redemption of the Black Athlete. He directs the Rhoden Fellows, a training program for aspiring journalists from HBCUs.

LaToya Sanders won a WNBA title as a player. Now she wants the same for the Atlanta Dream as a coach.

A WNBA champion as a player in 2019, the Dream assistant is considered a likely future head coach at the WNBA or college level

Sean Hurd @seanahurd

    By Jason Reid
  • Share on X (Opens in new window) X
  • Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook

On the afternoon of Game 3 of the WNBA semifinals last week, Atlanta Dream guard Rhyne Howard warmed up on a stationary bike just outside the visitors’ tunnel of the Barclays Center in Brooklyn, New York.

The Dream were one win shy of sweeping the New York Liberty and clinching the franchise’s first WNBA Finals appearance since 2013. Understandably, Howard appeared locked in, wearing a steady game face as she pedaled out the final moments of the team’s media availability before shootaround.

Her demeanor shifted after a question about the impact of LaToya Sanders, one of her assistant coaches. A full smile now radiated across Howard’s face as she sat back in her seat, her expression answering the question before she even said a word.

“My mom, she’s like, ‘[LaToya]’s your big sister.’ We’re so much alike. I think that’s what helps [LaToya] to keep me grounded,” Howard said. “I think she’s been perfect thus far. I hope that I can have her for the rest of my career.”

In her second season with the Dream, and her fifth as an assistant coach, Sanders has become a pivotal sideline contributor to Atlanta’s on-court success. Those close to Sanders, whose 12-year professional career included seven WNBA seasons and a 2019 championship, laud her basketball intellect and meticulous work ethic. Her pursuit of excellence in basketball, whether as a coach or a player, has been tireless.

Ultimately, her work is for one goal: to pull the best out of her players, to win a championship and one day, hopefully soon, to become a head coach. For now, she’s looking for her first title as an assistant.

“You sacrifice a lot as a player. You sacrifice a lot as a coach,” Sanders said. “To then come out with the ultimate prize, a championship, it would be wonderful.”

Among Sanders’ responsibilities is working individually with Howard and Angel Reese, two of the Dream’s All-Stars. She helps craft training plans and watches film with them, tailoring her presentations to highlight how they can use their skill sets to exploit defenses in upcoming games.

Sanders’ key to the pair’s success? Finding ways to elevate their teammates’ play.

“Both of them know that when other players get involved and have success, that the game is easier for them,” Sanders said. “We feel like no matter how good you are, there’s always areas that even the best players can improve in. We try to focus on those so they can be unstoppable.”

Howard lauded Sanders’ feedback style.

“I know that whatever she’s saying is not coming from a bad place,” Howard said. “The impact that she’s had on me, the impact that she’s had on Angel, I think has helped us become better players this year.”

One area Sanders has worked on with Reese is free throw shooting. During the playoffs, Reese has shot 87.1 percent from the line. In Game 2 against the Liberty, Reese came up big with multiple late-game free throw makes to secure the Dream’s overtime win. After the game, Reese referenced the free-throw regimen Sanders has crafted for her.

“I got to shoot 10 in a row with Toya. Last one got to be a swish coming right back to me,” Reese told Holly Rowe, a sideline reporter for ESPN and ABC.

Added Reese a few days later on Sanders: “We have honest conversations. We watch a lot of film. She’s been great for me.”

This weekend, Howard and Reese will make their WNBA Finals debuts. Until forward DeWanna Bonner arrived in late August, guards Jordin Canada and Shatori Walker-Kimbrough were the only players on the Atlanta roster to lift a WNBA championship trophy. As a result, Sanders — who understands the pressures of a Finals run after winning the 2019 title with the Washington Mystics — has been an integral resource for Dream players, answering their questions about what it takes to win in October.

“I know a lot of players on this team, [and] they really haven’t been out of the first round of the playoffs until this year,” Sanders said. “So understanding while that is an accomplishment, it’s not our end goal and we’re all going to just have to take a step forward to win a championship. I mean, it took me 12 years to get to the Finals — then 13 to win a championship. So, it’s not easy.”

Sanders’ role on the 2019 Mystics was that of the starting lineup’s reliable anchor, especially defensively. She was adaptable and could fill the gaps where the team needed her, helping the franchise to its first ring.

“She did all the little things,” said Dream guard Shatori Walker-Kimbrough, another member of the 2019 Mystics. “Whenever we needed her to step up, she definitely did that. We counted on her all the time defensively, and she always showed up.”

Beyond her time in the WNBA, Sanders had a formidable career overseas. She played alongside stars Diana Taurasi and Maya Moore in Russia and won the EuroLeague with UMMC Ekaterinburg in 2018. She became a naturalized Turkish citizen in 2012, representing the country at both the 2014 FIBA World Championships and the 2016 Rio Olympics.

Mike Thibault, the second-winningest coach in WNBA history, coached Sanders for four seasons in Washington. He said he always saw a future coach in her because of how she read the game.

“She was smart, as smart as players that I’ve had,” Thibault said. “She knew scouting reports, knew the game, and studied other players. She really, really studied the game.”

Thibault wasn’t sure, however, whether Sanders would be the “super outgoing” or “demonstrative” presence that coaching demands.

“I don’t think she knew if she was good enough at that, if she would let herself kind of go,” Thibault said. “When she and I talked about it, that was not a concern, but just something where she was [asking], ‘Are you sure I can do this?’”

Sanders joined Thibault’s coaching staff as an assistant in 2022. Just as she was during her playing days, Sanders was consistently the first person in the gym. Thibault remembers being impressed by her curiosity as a coach. In addition to the X’s and O’s, she expressed an interest in learning about the workings of the front office, from salary caps to trades.

“As a coach, that gives you an appreciation for all that has to go into building a roster, camaraderie and a culture,” Thibault said of Sanders, who was promoted to associate head coach in November 2022 and hired as an assistant with the Dream in 2025. “A lot of young coaches who come from being players assume they know a lot more, and she does not. … There’s a process to this, and [she] was willing to go through the process.”

Now in her fifth year on the sidelines, Sanders has seemingly found her voice. Thibault said Sanders has grown more comfortable standing up and saying what’s needed, while Walker-Kimbrough added that one of Sanders’ strengths is holding players accountable. Most importantly, Walker-Kimbrough said, Sanders does it authentically.

“I feel like sometimes when you’re trying to step into a new role, you kind of sometimes lose yourself or try to overdo it,” Walker-Kimbrough said. “[Sanders] has stayed herself and she’s been honest and she’s been blunt when she needs to be.”

Those around Sanders, from Thibault to Walker-Kimbrough to Dream head coach Karl Smesko, said she’s ready to take the next step in her coaching career.

“She’s ready to be a head coach right now,” Smesko told reporters last month. “She knows basketball at an exceptionally high level and she connects with people at an exceptionally high level. When you have those two things, you’re going to have a lot of success.”

Sanders continues to develop as a coach, even shadowing Atlanta Hawks practices during the offseason, but she is uncertain of her next step. While she enjoys her time with the Dream, she said she would never turn down a head coach opportunity — provided it is the right fit, including a potential move to the college ranks.

“I learned a lot from my coaching experiences in Washington, definitely for myself. I learned a lot from my coaching experience here with Karl so, yeah, you know I think I would be a good [head coach],” she said. “When that situation presents itself, I think I’ll be ready for it.”

As Sanders reflected on her journey in the league and her chance to win her first title as a coach, she thought about how much has changed in both her life and the WNBA since 2019. 

Standing on the sidelines of Barclays Center, Sanders recalled that the Liberty played in suburban Westchester County, not Brooklyn, in 2019. Back then, 4,000 fans watched the Mystics raise the WNBA championship trophy. Now, the Dream and Golden State Valkyries will play their Finals games in arenas seating more than 17,000.

And Sanders’ 5-year-old son, Semih Sway Sanders, wasn’t born yet — she would like to give him a championship experience.

“It’s kind of just like a full circle. I poured a lot into playing in the WNBA, made a lot of sacrifices, continue to make sacrifices, you know, as a coach. So, it’s the same feeling,” Sanders said. “I would love the opportunity to win the championship as both player and coach.”

Sean Hurd is a senior writer for Andscape who primarily covers women’s basketball. His athletic peak came at the age of 10 when he was named camper of the week at a Josh Childress basketball camp.

All-Black women’s roller derby team wants to bring a little ‘Black magic’ to global championships

‘When we play, there is a rhythm, there is chemistry’: Black Derby Collective skaters look to inspire inclusion in a largely white sport

Cliff Brunt @CliffBruntOG

Black Derby Collective didn’t expect to be this good this soon.

Founded barely a year ago, the all-Black women’s roller derby team rarely gets to practice because its skaters live all over the United States. Yet, they have thrived anyway with a chemistry members have called “Black magic.”

Black Derby Collective (BDC) won a regional playoff tournament in May to qualify for the Women’s Flat Track Derby Association (WFTDA) Championships this week in Malmö, Sweden. It’s the first all-Black team to reach the championship tournament in the WFTDA, the highest level of women’s roller derby in the world.

Maisha Cerqueda, a blocker who goes by the nickname Queen Loseyateefah, said the team’s connection is special.

“I know it sounds magical or mystical or ‘give it to the universe,’ but I do have to say that there is just something karmically tied between us that when we play. There is a rhythm, there is chemistry,” the Atlanta resident said. “I intuitively kind of know what some players are going to do. The way we play complements each other.”

The team is so new that it was unclear whether it would be able to play enough games to qualify for the regional.

“As the ancestors would have it,” Cerqueda said.

Black Derby Collective made it with the minimum five games necessary to qualify for regionals. It won the regional playoff in Columbia, South Carolina, in May to earn a trip to the global championships.

While Black Derby Collective wants to succeed on the track, its purpose goes further.

Dariann Hewson, a blocker and pivot who lives in Indianapolis and goes by the nickname Diamond, said she hopes the team inspires inclusion in a largely white sport.

“The goal for me is making sure that the opportunity is open for anyone who wants to play roller derby to do it safely and comfortably, because it’s not comfortable for everybody,” Hewson said.

Cerqueda said BDC’s emergence hasn’t been completely smooth.

“Some people are resistant to the fact that there’s even a Black team in the [roller derby] space,” she said. “I hope what people take about it is that there’s no substitution for being with your people, having a space where someone uniquely understands your experience here.”

Hewson said playing with a competitive, all-Black team is a long way from her early days of playing noncompetitive roller derby on a predominantly white team in Anderson, Indiana.

“I played with a team that wasn’t ranked,” she said. “We had zero or minimal goals outside of just having a good time and showing up to the afterparty. If we lost the game, we won that.”

Hewson switched to an Indianapolis-based team to get better competition, and now she’s on a roller derby team with an Olympic gold medalist.

Speedskater Erin Jackson is best known for becoming the first Black woman to win an individual gold medal at the Winter Olympics, a feat she achieved in 2022 in Beijing. While she has been speedskating since 2017, she has been playing roller derby since 2012.

Though Jackson is currently injured and unable to compete, she enjoys simply being around Black Derby Collective.

“Just having that community on the team and on the track, being able to look left, look right, and then see people who look like you — it’s a really, really rare thing for what I do,” Jackson said.

Jackson has relished being a part of the team as its members build a connection.

“People who don’t really follow roller derby, they might not understand how impressive that is by just having all these skaters who can, in a way, read each other’s minds and know where to be and how to work together,” she said.

It’s not just about the players all being Black. Hewson said many of them didn’t fit into mainstream sports as kids and have found roller derby to be an outlet as adults. She said it’s also a place where quirkiness is welcome.

“I’m a little bit of a weirdo, so I never fit in with the normal sports. … I went to my first [roller derby] practice and met a lot of people who were very similar to me, a lot of people on the spectrum, and people who had similar brains to mine,” Hewson said. “So I love being able to be a part of a group of people.”

The players don’t get paid — BDC is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit — and are making familial, career and financial sacrifices to fulfill their championship dreams.

“This one just feels different because I’m doing it with a group of people who may not have the opportunity where they’re at, and we have made a decision to do it together, no matter the cost, no matter the travel, no matter the time,” Hewson said.

Roller derby is known for players’ colorful nicknames. Other BDC nicknames include Blaxyl Rose, Poison Violet, Murda, Blacque Jac, PuRRfect, Ima Blow Bya and Trouble MakeHer.

Now this collection of Black skaters from cities such as Los Angeles, Seattle and Atlanta has a chance to pursue the Hydra — the trophy that goes to the world’s best team — after playing together for only five games, with no practice time.

“A lot of my teammates are younger in roller derby, so they don’t realize that this is not normal,” Cerqueda said. “You shouldn’t be able to just pull 20 people together and do amazing things if you don’t normally play together.

“If we can thread this needle and make this happen, it’ll be amazing. If we’re not able to do that, that’s totally fine, because we know it’s just our first year of being a team.”

Cliff Brunt has been a sportswriter since the '90s, including a run of more than 20 years with The Associated Press. He is an Omaha North High Viking of Distinction who received Creighton University's Alumni Merit Award in 2025.

For the Los Angeles Rams, the clock is ticking

From Super Bowl favorite to frustrated, Rams facing defense, special teams questions after OT loss to Bills

Jason Reid @JReidESPN
October 13, 2026
Topics:
Buffalo Bills Los Angeles Rams NFL Sports

    For the Los Angeles Rams, the clock is ticking

    By Jason Reid
  • Share on X (Opens in new window) X
  • Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook
  • Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email

INGLEWOOD, Calif. — While the Los Angeles Rams remain confident, their march to potential greatness is proceeding slowly.

Already frustrated with whom they see in the mirror, the Rams had even more to dislike after a 37-34 overtime loss to the Buffalo Bills on “Monday Night Football.”

After rallying to tie the score at 34 on a touchdown with five seconds remaining in regulation, the Rams’ 48-yard field-goal attempt that would’ve won the game in overtime was blocked, capping yet another horrendous special teams performance. Facing Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen, the defense’s showing was also unsettling.

The Rams repeatedly failed to contain the gifted runner in the pocket, and Allen’s legs powered the Bills on the game’s decisive drive. In total, Allen led the Bills with 121 rushing yards on only 10 attempts, and he put them in position for kicker Tyler Bass to end the game with a 45-yard field goal.

After Week 5, the Rams, the overwhelming preseason favorites to win Super Bowl LXI, are 2-3 overall and 1-2 at SoFi Stadium – their home field where the Super Bowl will be played in February. At the moment, however, the Rams are focused on achieving modest goals.

Getting back to basics on special teams, executing better on offense and holding it together on defense until dominant edge rusher Myles Garrett returns from injured reserve top a busy to-do list for head coach Sean McVay and his staff.

On Monday, McVay did not sugarcoat his assessment of where things stand for the underachieving group he leads.

“This, this one is … this is the one that stinks, and it’s gonna hurt,” he said. “It’s been a while since I’ve been this pissed after a game, too.”

Although his mood was ruined by so much, let’s start with special teams.

The unit was such an embarrassment last season that McVay worked overtime in the offseason to fix it. As with many areas on the Rams, that rebuilding project is still in progress.

On Monday, Bills backup running back Ray Davis returned the opening kickoff 70 yards to help set up a Bass field goal. On the Rams’ ensuing possession, kicker Harrison Mevis missed a 50-yard attempt. And more than three hours later, with the game on the line in overtime, the Bills blocked Los Angeles’ would-be game-winner.

“I felt like I hit it good,” Mevis said of the blocked kick. “I mean, I hit it good, gave it a chance. They had good rush teams.”

Similarly, Mevis was optimistic about his missed kick in the first quarter. Well, initially, anyway.

“I feel like I hit it solid, [I] just came around it a little bit, pushed it to the left,” he said. “Gotta be fixed. Gotta make those. Gotta go back to the training ground.”

The Rams have a lot to review on defense, too.

Rams House brings taste of Southern California to Australia – Andscape Read now

There’s no shame in being torched by Allen in the running game. He’s one of the greatest dual-threat quarterbacks in NFL history.

That established, the Rams needed to be more disciplined in maintaining their rush lanes against Allen, better at containing him in the pocket and more efficient at tackling him when they got hands on him. Obviously, accomplishing all of that is easier in theory in meeting rooms than on the field.

Allen produced 331 yards of offense — including 210 passing yards — and two touchdowns. Running back James Cook rushed for 111 yards and two touchdowns on 25 carries. The Bills racked up 234 yards on the ground.

As the Rams put it bluntly, not good.

Allen, as is usually the case for Buffalo’s opponents, was the biggest problem.

“We made a lot of mistakes,” outside linebacker Byron Young said. “[Allen] ran for [121] yards, and that basically won them the game. He was getting good field position, getting positive yards. Just us as a D-line, we gotta be better. We know how to rush — and that’s unacceptable. If we want to win games … we can’t let that happen.”

At least defensively for the Rams, major help may be coming soon.

Garrett, who underwent arthroscopic knee surgery in mid-September, is “making good progress,” McVay told reporters recently. His potential return to the lineup early next month could be a game changer for a group that needs one.

Additionally, future Hall of Fame defensive lineman Aaron Donald, who came out of retirement this season, was disruptive against the Bills. Cornerback Jaylen Watson, a key part of the Rams’ secondary makeover in the offseason, had an interception Monday.

On offense, quarterback Matthew Stafford (383 passing yards, three touchdown passes) and wide receiver Puka Nacua (17 receptions, 138 yards, one touchdown) had monster games. There’s no doubt about it: The Rams are loaded.

McVay sees potential for greatness. But the potential must materialize — soon.

“None of it makes me feel good right now,” he said. “Other than I’m proud of the effort.”

Of course, that alone won’t get the Rams to where many predicted they’ll finish the season. And the clock is ticking.

Jason Reid is the senior NFL writer at Andscape. He enjoys watching sports, especially any games involving his son and daughter.
